text: In David Lewis's 'Elusive Knowledge,' the Rule of Attention accounts for the force of skepticism by holding that:
choices: a possibility that is explicitly attended to or mentioned thereby becomes relevant and must be eliminated, so raising the brain-in-a-vat scenario destroys the knowledge one would otherwise have
a belief counts as knowledge only if it would track the truth across the nearest possible worlds
a subject must rule out only those alternatives made salient by the practical stakes they actually face
the reference of 'brain' is fixed by the subject's causal contact with the environment
explanation: Lewis analyzes knowledge as the elimination of every uneliminated possibility, subject to a Rule of Attention: merely attending to a possibility (such as the BIV) makes it relevant, so it must now be eliminated—which cannot be done, and knowledge slips away. Option 1 is Nozick's tracking, option 2 is pragmatic encroachment / subject-sensitive invariantism, and option 3 is Putnam's semantic externalism.
